task: Write one sentence of your own using the word grandiloquence. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know grandiloquence should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The menu's grandiloquence was legendary: a grilled cheese arrived as 'artisanal hearth-kissed curds embraced by heritage grain.'
Polish is simply care — smooth sentences, good rhythm; it stops far short of grandiloquence and usually improves a speech.
Floweriness goes further than polish, draping blossoms of ornament over every noun, but grandiloquence tops this ladder: the ornament turns pompous and the meaning disappears under it.

Bombast is noisy, inflated language — speech that booms and swaggers to impress a room. Grandiloquence lives in the word choice itself: lofty, self-important phrasing that can be delivered in a whisper. Bombast is a fault of volume and force; grandiloquence is a fault of costume.

Pomposity is self-importance in a person's whole manner — the slow nod, the lofty tone, the air of addressing lesser beings, with or without fancy words. Grandiloquence is the vocabulary pomposity reaches for: the inflated wording itself. A pompous man can sit silent; grandiloquence needs a sentence.
saying the thing in the words it needs, no costume
aiming straight at the point without ornament
Every actor in the company covets the role with the great soliloquy in the third act.
Grandiloquence means lofty, pompous language.
The debate coach let the freshman finish his opening — 'we stand at the fulcrum of history's eternal pendulum' — then circled one word on her clipboard: grandiloquence.
'The judges,' she said, 'award points for arguments.
Give them one plain sentence with a fact in it.'
Grandiloquence is language dressed above its station: lofty, pompous wording chosen to sound magnificent rather than to say something.
Eloquence moves an audience; grandiloquence performs for it, and listeners usually hear the difference within a sentence.
Grandiloquence is a critic's word — you diagnose it in someone else's inflated speech.
Bombast stresses noise, pomposity stresses self-importance, and turgid, this unit's adjective for swollen prose, describes the style itself; grandiloquence names the lofty wording.
None of them are compliments.

Our landlord's renovation notices are a neighborhood entertainment.

No pipe is ever repaired in them; plumbing 'undergoes a renaissance.' The lobby was not repainted last spring -- it 'ascended toward its destiny in eggshell white.' My neighbor tapes each notice to her refrigerator, and we have learned to translate the grandiloquence at a glance: the loftier the phrasing, the smaller the actual work.
When the elevator broke, the notice promised 'a majestic vertical renewal.' A repairman came Tuesday and replaced a fuse.
We suspect the man writes this way everywhere, wishing his nephews 'a splendid commencement of their ninth year.'
